Hyperthyroidism is caused by Grave's disease which is an autoimmune disease.  The hallmark of Grave's disease is the production of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor mimicking antibodies which stimulate the thyroid to produce excess thyroid hormones.  Excess thyroid hormones can cause the symptoms seen in this patient.  The main treatments for Grave's disease are antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole or propylthiouracil (PTU) which inhibit thyroid hormones, radioactive iodine which destroys thyroid tissue and surgery (thyroidectomy).  Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis so it is contraindicated in Grave's disease.  Iodine excess can also cause or exacerbate other conditions such as the storm (a life threatening hyperthyroid state).  Hypothyroidism is treated with thyroid hormone replacement therapy either with T4 (levothyroxine) or T3.  Diabetes is treated with insulin.  Cortisol is a glucocorticoid and hydrocortisone is used to treat adrenal insufficiency.

The answer is the foramen ovale. This is part of a whole that includes the ductus arteriosus and the fossa ovalis.  The foramen ovale is an opening between the left and right atria in the foetal heart. This allows the oxygenated blood from the placenta to bypass the foetal lungs and enter the left atria. After birth, this closes to become the fossa ovalis.  The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta. After birth, this closes to become the ligamentum arteriosum.  Other structures that disappear include the left umbilical vein which becomes the left coronary vein and the left auricle which becomes the fossa ovalis (this is different to the fossa ovalis, which is part of the heart and the fossa ovalis is part of the foetal heart).  Source: Essential clinical anatomy and physiology, case 8.

Calsequestrin is the correct answer. It is found in the ryanodine receptor of the SR and sequesters Ca2+ by binding to it. This prevents the receptor opening prematurely. Increased Ca2+ in the cell (ie. via L-type Ca2+ channels during a cardiac action potential) removes this effect and causes calcium-induced-calcium release.  Calbindin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in the ER of cells in smooth muscle. It increases the total Ca2+ stored in the ER. Calmodulin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in the cytosol of cells in smooth muscle. It regulates various motor proteins and other enzymes. Phospholamban is a Ca2+ sensitive protein that regulates the uptake of calcium into the SR. When dephosphorylated, it inhibits SERCA and prevents Ca2+ uptake into the SR. When phosphorylated, it is inactive and allows Ca2+ uptake into the SR. SERCA is a Ca2+ pump that pumps Ca2+ into the SR.

The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim that surrounds the glenoid fossa and is made of dense irregular connective tissue and fibrocartilage. It is attached to the rim of the socket and deepens the socket to improve the congruence between the head of the humerus and the glenoid fossa.
